questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between the deepagents package and create_agent?

options.text: deepagents is a separate package built on top of create_agent's core building blocks, not a replacement for it.
deepagents is a drop-in replacement that fully supersedes create_agent, which vendors now recommend avoiding for new projects.
deepagents and create_agent are unrelated packages maintained by different organizations with no shared foundation or dependency.
create_agent is an internal helper that deepagents exposes only after a project has already adopted the deepagents harness.

questions.explanation: deepagents is a separate package built on top of create_agent's core building blocks, not a replacement for it.

optionExplanations.pa-q01-opt-a: deepagents is documented as a separate package that layers additional capabilities on top of create_agent's foundational building blocks, rather than replacing that foundation.
optionExplanations.pa-q01-opt-b: There is no supersession relationship; create_agent remains the recommended choice for lightweight, low-level agent building and is not being phased out in favor of deepagents.
optionExplanations.pa-q01-opt-c: deepagents depends on and builds directly on create_agent's core loop, so the two are not unrelated packages from different organizations with no shared foundation.
optionExplanations.pa-q01-opt-d: create_agent is the standalone, lower-level builder function that exists independently of deepagents; deepagents consumes it as a foundation rather than exposing it only after adoption.

questions.takeaway: deepagents is a separate package built on top of create_agent's core building blocks, not a replacement for it.

questions.stem: A platform team is building their own opinionated agent framework on top of LangChain and wants to assemble every component themselves rather than inherit a pre-built harness. Which builder aligns with that goal?

options.text: create_agent, since it offers explicit low-level control with minimal defaults for teams that want to define each component themselves.
deepagents, since its harness exposes every middleware and tool as fully optional, making it functionally equivalent to assembling components individually.
create_agent, since it forces adoption of filesystem tools, skills loading, and sub-agent spawning that cannot be turned off.
deepagents, since it is the only builder that supports customizing the underlying LangGraph runtime for a bespoke framework.

questions.explanation: create_agent, since it offers explicit low-level control with minimal defaults for teams that want to define each component themselves.

optionExplanations.pa-q02-opt-a: create_agent's minimal defaults and low-level control are exactly suited to a platform team that wants to hand-assemble every component of its own opinionated framework.
optionExplanations.pa-q02-opt-b: deepagents is described as an opinionated harness with capabilities bundled in by default; that is a different design goal from a team wanting to assemble every piece itself from a minimal base.
optionExplanations.pa-q02-opt-c: create_agent does not force adoption of filesystem tools, skills loading, or sub-agent spawning; those are deepagents harness features layered on top, not mandatory parts of create_agent.
optionExplanations.pa-q02-opt-d: Both builders ultimately run on the same LangGraph runtime, and deepagents is not uniquely positioned to customize that runtime for a bespoke framework; create_agent's minimal defaults are what serve this goal.

questions.takeaway: create_agent, since it offers explicit low-level control with minimal defaults for teams that want to define each component themselves.

questions.stem: An agent is configured with two middleware instances, registered in the order `[AuthMiddleware, LoggingMiddleware]`, each implementing both `before_model` and `after_model` hooks. In what order do the `after_model` hooks execute relative to each other?

options.text: `LoggingMiddleware.after_model` runs, then `AuthMiddleware.after_model` runs, the reverse of their registration order.
`AuthMiddleware.after_model` runs, then `LoggingMiddleware.after_model` runs, matching their registration order.
Both `after_model` hooks run simultaneously in parallel, since after hooks have no defined ordering guarantee.
Only the last-registered middleware's `after_model` hook runs; earlier middleware hooks are skipped for that phase.

questions.explanation: `LoggingMiddleware.after_model` runs, then `AuthMiddleware.after_model` runs, the reverse of their registration order.

optionExplanations.pa-q03-opt-a: This is correct because after hooks execute in reverse of the middleware registration order, so the last-registered middleware's `after_model` runs first and the first-registered runs last.
optionExplanations.pa-q03-opt-b: This is incorrect because that is the order for `before_model` hooks, which run in registration order; `after_model` hooks run in the opposite, reverse order.
optionExplanations.pa-q03-opt-c: This is incorrect because node-style hooks execute sequentially in a defined order, not concurrently, so there is no race between the two `after_model` calls.
optionExplanations.pa-q03-opt-d: This is incorrect because every registered middleware's `after_model` hook runs on each pass; none are skipped simply because another middleware is also registered.

questions.takeaway: `LoggingMiddleware.after_model` runs, then `AuthMiddleware.after_model` runs, the reverse of their registration order.

questions.stem: A fintech agent handles customer chats that may contain account numbers, executes a `wire_transfer` tool that should require human approval, and must not let a single conversation trigger unlimited transfer attempts. Which middleware components should the team combine to meet all three requirements? (Select all that apply.) (Select 3)

options.text: `PIIMiddleware` configured to detect and redact account-number patterns in conversation messages.
`HumanInTheLoopMiddleware` configured with `interrupt_on` scoped to the `wire_transfer` tool.
`ToolCallLimitMiddleware` scoped to the `wire_transfer` tool with a `thread_limit`.
`ModelFallbackMiddleware` configured with backup models for when the primary provider is unavailable.
`LLMToolEmulator` configured to emulate the `wire_transfer` tool during production traffic.
`TodoListMiddleware` configured to track the agent's task list across the conversation.

questions.explanation: A: `PIIMiddleware` directly addresses protecting account numbers by detecting and redacting sensitive patterns in the conversation. | B: Scoping `HumanInTheLoopMiddleware`'s `interrupt_on` to the `wire_transfer` tool pauses that specific tool for human approval before it executes. | C: A per-tool `thread_limit` on `ToolCallLimitMiddleware` caps how many times `wire_transfer` can be invoked within a single conversation, preventing unlimited attempts.

optionExplanations.pa-q04-opt-a: `PIIMiddleware` directly addresses protecting account numbers by detecting and redacting sensitive patterns in the conversation.
optionExplanations.pa-q04-opt-b: Scoping `HumanInTheLoopMiddleware`'s `interrupt_on` to the `wire_transfer` tool pauses that specific tool for human approval before it executes.
optionExplanations.pa-q04-opt-c: A per-tool `thread_limit` on `ToolCallLimitMiddleware` caps how many times `wire_transfer` can be invoked within a single conversation, preventing unlimited attempts.
optionExplanations.pa-q04-opt-d: Incorrect — `ModelFallbackMiddleware` addresses model provider outages, not PII protection, approval workflows, or capping tool invocation counts.
optionExplanations.pa-q04-opt-e: Incorrect — `LLMToolEmulator` is meant for testing by replacing real tool execution with simulated responses, which would be unsafe and inappropriate for production wire transfers.
optionExplanations.pa-q04-opt-f: Incorrect — `TodoListMiddleware` equips an agent with task planning and tracking, which does not address PII protection, approvals, or invocation limits.

questions.takeaway: `PIIMiddleware` directly addresses protecting account numbers by detecting and redacting sensitive patterns in the conversation.

questions.stem: A team member creates a new skill directory named `pdf-summarizer` but writes `name: pdf_summarizer` in the SKILL.md frontmatter. At agent startup, the skill fails validation. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The `name` field must be lowercase alphanumeric with hyphens and exactly match the parent directory name, and underscores break that match.
The `description` field is missing, so the skill can't register regardless of the `name` value that was chosen.
Skill folders require a `scripts/` subdirectory before frontmatter parsing begins, and this skill omitted that required subfolder.
The `allowed-tools` field becomes mandatory whenever a skill's `name` differs from its folder path, and this skill left it out.

questions.explanation: The `name` field must be lowercase alphanumeric with hyphens and exactly match the parent directory name, and underscores break that match.

optionExplanations.pa-q05-opt-a: The `name` field is defined as a lowercase alphanumeric identifier with hyphens that must exactly match the parent directory name; using an underscore instead of a hyphen produces a mismatch and fails validation.
optionExplanations.pa-q05-opt-b: Nothing in the scenario indicates the `description` field was omitted, so a missing description is not the cause of this particular failure.
optionExplanations.pa-q05-opt-c: There is no requirement that a skill folder contain a `scripts/` subdirectory; supporting folders like scripts, references, and assets are optional additions, not prerequisites for parsing.
optionExplanations.pa-q05-opt-d: There is no rule tying `allowed-tools` to whether `name` matches the folder path; `allowed-tools` is an independent, optional field for pre-approving tool access.

questions.takeaway: The `name` field must be lowercase alphanumeric with hyphens and exactly match the parent directory name, and underscores break that match.

questions.stem: To avoid bloating the system prompt when dozens of skills are configured, only two frontmatter fields are injected into the system prompt for every skill at agent startup, with the rest of each SKILL.md loaded only if that skill is triggered. Which two fields are these?

options.text: `name` and `description`
`name` and `allowed-tools`
`description` and `compatibility`
`name` and `license`

questions.explanation: `name` and `description`

optionExplanations.pa-q06-opt-a: Only the `name` and `description` fields are injected into the system prompt for every configured skill at startup, which lets the agent discover skills without paying the token cost of every full body.
optionExplanations.pa-q06-opt-b: `allowed-tools` is not part of the startup metadata injection; it governs which tools a skill may call once it has been activated and its body has been read.
optionExplanations.pa-q06-opt-c: `compatibility` describes environment requirements and is not one of the two fields injected at startup for every skill.
optionExplanations.pa-q06-opt-d: `license` records licensing terms and is not part of the startup metadata; it is only relevant once the full skill body is loaded.

questions.takeaway: `name` and `description`.

questions.stem: In LangChain's context-engineering guidance for long-running agents, what is the key architectural difference between message trimming and the `SummarizationMiddleware` summarization approach?

options.text: Trimming drops older messages for one model call without touching state, while summarization permanently overwrites state with a generated summary.
Trimming permanently deletes older messages from state entirely, while summarization only hides them briefly during a single isolated model call.
Trimming needs an LLM to condense messages, while summarization discards messages using only token-count heuristics and never a model.
Both approaches persist their changes to state in precisely the same way, differing only in which underlying model actually produces the replacement text.

questions.explanation: Trimming drops older messages for one model call without touching state, while summarization permanently overwrites state with a generated summary.

optionExplanations.pa-q07-opt-a: Trimming is a transient, per-call adjustment that never writes back to state, while summarization is persistent — it replaces older messages in state with a generated summary so future turns see the summary instead of the originals.
optionExplanations.pa-q07-opt-b: Reverses the mechanics: trimming does not touch state at all, and summarization is the one that persists a permanent change, not a temporary one.
optionExplanations.pa-q07-opt-c: Trimming uses simple heuristics like keeping the most recent K messages and requires no LLM call; it is summarization that relies on a model to condense older turns.
optionExplanations.pa-q07-opt-d: Trimming never persists anything to state — only summarization writes a permanent replacement — so the two approaches do not behave identically with respect to state.

questions.takeaway: Trimming drops older messages for one model call without touching state, while summarization permanently overwrites state with a generated summary.

questions.stem: A team debugging a long-running support agent notices that after several summarization cycles, the agent contradicts facts stated at the very start of the conversation, while still performing well on tasks from recent turns. Which explanations are consistent with how `SummarizationMiddleware` operates? (Select 2)

options.text: Once messages fall outside the `keep` window, only the generated summary represents them, so nuanced early details can be lost during condensation.
The summary permanently replaces the original older messages in state, so any information the summarization step dropped is not recoverable from that state.
The middleware re-reads the full original transcript from a separate log on every turn, so summarization cannot cause information loss like this.
Recent messages inside the `keep` window are also condensed into the summary, which is why contradictions appear even in the latest turns.
The summarization model always achieves perfect lossless compression, so any contradiction must come from a prompt or tool bug elsewhere.

questions.explanation: A: Details outside the preserved window exist only through the generated summary, so any nuance the summarization step failed to capture is genuinely gone from the model's view. | B: Because summarization permanently overwrites state, once information is lost during condensation there is no original copy left in state to recover it from on later turns.

optionExplanations.pa-q08-opt-a: Details outside the preserved window exist only through the generated summary, so any nuance the summarization step failed to capture is genuinely gone from the model's view.
optionExplanations.pa-q08-opt-b: Because summarization permanently overwrites state, once information is lost during condensation there is no original copy left in state to recover it from on later turns.
optionExplanations.pa-q08-opt-c: Incorrect — there is no separate always-consulted transcript log; the middleware relies on the summary once older messages are condensed, so it can indeed lose information this way.
optionExplanations.pa-q08-opt-d: Incorrect — messages inside the `keep` window retain their original form and are not condensed, so contradictions on early facts are not explained by recent-turn messages being summarized.
optionExplanations.pa-q08-opt-e: Incorrect — summarization is lossy by nature since it condenses content through a model, so assuming perfect lossless compression contradicts the observed behavior of losing early details.

questions.takeaway: Details outside the preserved window exist only through the generated summary, so any nuance the summarization step failed to capture is genuinely gone from the model's view.

questions.stem: An agent's sandbox integration is implemented as a subclass that only overrides `execute()`, relying on `BaseSandbox` for everything else, yet the agent still gets working `ls`, `grep`, and `edit_file` tools. Which explanation accounts for this?

options.text: `BaseSandbox` constructs the scripts for each filesystem operation and runs them through the subclass's `execute()` implementation
Those tools are unrelated to the sandbox subclass and are wired in separately by the model provider
`ls`, `grep`, and `edit_file` are implemented as no-op stubs that always return empty results in any sandbox
The subclass must also separately override each filesystem method for them to function, contradicting the premise

questions.explanation: `BaseSandbox` constructs the scripts for each filesystem operation and runs them through the subclass's `execute()` implementation.

optionExplanations.pa-q09-opt-a: `BaseSandbox` builds the scripts needed for operations like `ls`, `grep`, and `edit_file` and runs them through the single `execute()` method, so a subclass only needs to implement `execute()` for all of these filesystem tools to work.
optionExplanations.pa-q09-opt-b: Incorrect — these filesystem tools are part of the sandbox backend abstraction itself, implemented on top of `execute()`, not something wired in independently by a model provider.
optionExplanations.pa-q09-opt-c: Incorrect — these tools run real generated scripts against the sandbox and return actual results; they are not stub implementations that always return empty output.
optionExplanations.pa-q09-opt-d: Incorrect — `BaseSandbox` deliberately implements filesystem operations on top of a single `execute()` primitive precisely so subclasses do not need to reimplement each filesystem method individually.

questions.takeaway: `BaseSandbox` constructs the scripts for each filesystem operation and runs them through the subclass's `execute()` implementation.

questions.stem: A security review of a sandboxed coding agent concludes that the sandbox successfully stops the agent from touching the host filesystem or host processes. The reviewer still flags a residual risk: a malicious document the agent reads during a task could instruct it to run destructive commands inside the sandbox itself. Why does sandboxing not eliminate this risk?

options.text: Sandboxing isolates the agent from the host system but does not prevent context injection attacks that make the agent issue harmful commands within its own isolated environment.
Sandboxing only restricts the agent's outbound network traffic and does not filter file contents, so instructions hidden in a document the agent reads are never executed inside the environment.
The `execute()` primitive automatically screens every shell command the agent submits for malicious intent and blocks destructive ones before they run, so poisoned documents cannot cause damage.
Context injection is impossible once a sandbox is configured, because the isolated environment strips untrusted document content before the agent reads it, so the reviewer's concern does not apply.

questions.explanation: Sandboxing isolates the agent from the host system but does not prevent context injection attacks that make the agent issue harmful commands within its own isolated environment.

optionExplanations.pa-q10-opt-a: A sandbox isolates the agent from the host filesystem and host processes, but it does not control what the agent decides to do inside its own environment. A malicious document the agent reads can inject instructions into its context and lead it to issue destructive commands within the sandbox, which is why this residual risk remains.
optionExplanations.pa-q10-opt-b: Incorrect — sandboxing is not limited to restricting outbound network traffic. Its documented scope is filesystem and process isolation from the host. The claim that hidden instructions are never executed inside the environment is also false.
optionExplanations.pa-q10-opt-c: Incorrect — the `execute()` primitive is a generic command-execution method with no built-in screening for malicious intent. It runs whatever command or script it is given and returns the output.
optionExplanations.pa-q10-opt-d: Incorrect — context injection remains possible with a sandbox configured, because the sandbox does not strip or sanitize untrusted document content before the agent reads it. Sandbox outputs should be treated as untrusted and paired with additional controls.

questions.takeaway: Sandboxing isolates the agent from the host system but does not prevent context injection attacks that make the agent issue harmful commands within its own isolated environment.

questions.stem: A platform team is documenting how graphs and deployments relate to each other in Agent Server. Which of the following statements are accurate? (Select all that apply.) (Select 3)

optionExplanations.pa-q19-opt-b: The same graph's code can serve as the basis for multiple deployments, such as separate staging and production instances, each with its own configuration.

optionExplanations.pa-q19-opt-e: A deployment's revision history tracks its own version number independently of the graph's source code.

questions.stem: Which of the following are recommended practices for handling API keys and tokens used by a deployed LangGraph agent? (Select all that apply.) (Select 3)

options.text: Load credentials from environment variables or a secret management service rather than embedding them in code.
Configure production secrets through the deployment platform's settings so they are scoped per revision.
Commit a `.env` file containing production keys to the repository so the whole team can access it.
Rotate a credential and redeploy whenever there is any indication that the value may have been exposed.
Print credential values to application logs during startup so operators can confirm they loaded correctly.
Paste credential values into chat messages when a teammate needs temporary access for testing.

questions.explanation: A: Loading credentials from environment variables or a secret management service is the core recommended pattern for keeping sensitive values out of source code. | B: Configuring production secrets through deployment platform settings scoped per revision keeps credential changes tracked and applied through a controlled redeploy process. | D: Rotating a credential and redeploying once exposure is suspected limits the window during which a compromised key remains usable.

optionExplanations.pa-q20-opt-a: Loading credentials from environment variables or a secret management service is the core recommended pattern for keeping sensitive values out of source code.
optionExplanations.pa-q20-opt-b: Configuring production secrets through deployment platform settings scoped per revision keeps credential changes tracked and applied through a controlled redeploy process.
optionExplanations.pa-q20-opt-c: Committing a `.env` file with production keys exposes those credentials to everyone with repository access and permanently to the commit history.
optionExplanations.pa-q20-opt-d: Rotating a credential and redeploying once exposure is suspected limits the window during which a compromised key remains usable.

optionExplanations.pa-q20-opt-f: Pasting credential values into chat messages creates an unmanaged, unauditable copy of the secret outside any access-controlled system.

questions.stem: Which statements about how LangGraph Platform handles secrets across deployment revisions are accurate? (Select all that apply) (Select 3)

options.text: Secrets can be set independently for each revision, so a new revision can introduce or change a credential value.
Rotating a credential typically requires creating a new revision through a redeploy rather than a live in-place edit.
Every revision automatically inherits any change made to a later revision's secrets without additional configuration.
Runs and threads created under an earlier revision continue to reflect the environment that revision was deployed with.
Secret values configured in the deployment settings are stored in plaintext inside the checked-in `langgraph.json`.

questions.explanation: A: Secrets are scoped per revision, so each new revision can introduce a new credential or change an existing one independently of prior revisions. | B: Because secret changes apply to a new revision rather than being live-patched onto a running one, rotating a credential normally requires triggering a redeploy. | D: Runs and threads tied to an earlier revision keep using that revision's environment, which is why an older run can still reflect a since-rotated credential.

optionExplanations.pa-q21-opt-a: Secrets are scoped per revision, so each new revision can introduce a new credential or change an existing one independently of prior revisions.
optionExplanations.pa-q21-opt-b: Because secret changes apply to a new revision rather than being live-patched onto a running one, rotating a credential normally requires triggering a redeploy.
optionExplanations.pa-q21-opt-c: Revisions do not automatically inherit later secret changes; each revision keeps the environment it was created with unless it is itself redeployed.
optionExplanations.pa-q21-opt-d: Runs and threads tied to an earlier revision keep using that revision's environment, which is why an older run can still reflect a since-rotated credential.
optionExplanations.pa-q21-opt-e: Secrets configured through deployment settings are managed by the platform separately from `langgraph.json`, not stored in plaintext inside the checked-in configuration file.

questions.stem: A team redeploys their Agent Server, changing `LANGGRAPH_HOST_URL` from the default endpoint to the EU endpoint so new traffic is served from the EU. What happens to the deployment's existing threads that were created before this change?

options.text: A new revision is created with the EU endpoint going forward, but existing threads already persisted under the prior configuration are not relocated by this change alone.
All existing threads are automatically migrated to EU-region PostgreSQL storage as part of the same redeploy operation.
The redeploy is rejected because `LANGGRAPH_HOST_URL` cannot be changed once a deployment has active threads.
Existing threads become permanently inaccessible the moment the endpoint changes, since revisions do not retain references to prior configurations.

questions.explanation: A new revision is created with the EU endpoint going forward, but existing threads already persisted under the prior configuration are not relocated by this change alone.

optionExplanations.pa-q22-opt-a: Redeploying with a changed environment variable produces a new revision that governs configuration going forward, but there is no documented step in that process that relocates already-persisted thread data to a different region's storage.
optionExplanations.pa-q22-opt-b: No automatic thread migration between regions is part of a redeploy operation; changing the host URL affects new configuration, not existing persisted data.
optionExplanations.pa-q22-opt-c: Revisions are the standard mechanism for changing a deployment's environment variables and secrets over time, including variables like the host URL.
optionExplanations.pa-q22-opt-d: Existing threads remain in their original backing store and are not described as becoming inaccessible; a revision changes configuration going forward without destroying prior persisted state.

questions.takeaway: A new revision is created with the EU endpoint going forward, but existing threads already persisted under the prior configuration are not relocated by this change alone.

questions.stem: EU-based users report elevated latency when using an agent whose Cloud deployment was created without specifying `LANGGRAPH_HOST_URL`. What is the most likely cause and fix?

options.text: The deployment is running on the default (non-EU) endpoint; redeploying with `LANGGRAPH_HOST_URL` set to the EU endpoint routes new traffic through EU-hosted infrastructure.
The deployment's queue worker count is too low; adding more workers to the existing region will resolve cross-continental latency regardless of hosting location.
The `LANGSMITH_AUTH_TYPE` variable is misconfigured; switching it to `noop` removes an authentication round-trip that is causing the delay.
The deployment's checkpointer `durability` mode is set to `sync`; switching to `exit` mode reduces network latency for EU requests.

questions.explanation: The deployment is running on the default (non-EU) endpoint; redeploying with `LANGGRAPH_HOST_URL` set to the EU endpoint routes new traffic through EU-hosted infrastructure.

optionExplanations.pa-q23-opt-a: Without explicitly setting `LANGGRAPH_HOST_URL`, a Cloud deployment defaults to its standard (non-EU) hosting region, so EU users end up making cross-continental requests; redeploying with the EU endpoint moves the hosting location closer to them.
optionExplanations.pa-q23-opt-b: Adding queue workers increases processing throughput within the deployment's existing region, but it does not shorten the network distance data travels.
optionExplanations.pa-q23-opt-c: `LANGSMITH_AUTH_TYPE` controls how requests are authenticated, not where the deployment's infrastructure is physically located.
optionExplanations.pa-q23-opt-d: The `durability` parameter controls when checkpoint writes are considered persisted during graph execution — a correctness/performance tradeoff unrelated to which region serves EU network requests.

questions.takeaway: The deployment is running on the default (non-EU) endpoint; redeploying with `LANGGRAPH_HOST_URL` set to the EU endpoint routes new traffic through EU-hosted infrastructure.

questions.stem: In the context of a LangSmith Deployment (Agent Server), what is the core conceptual distinction between authentication and authorization?

options.text: Authentication confirms who is making a request, while authorization decides what that already-identified caller may do.
Authentication decides what a caller may do, while authorization confirms that the caller's credentials are not expired.
Authentication filters which threads a caller can list, while authorization only validates the caller's network origin.
Authentication and authorization both verify identity, differing only in whether the check runs before or after a run completes.

questions.explanation: Authentication confirms who is making a request, while authorization decides what that already-identified caller may do.

optionExplanations.pa-q24-opt-a: An authentication handler establishes identity on every request, and separate authorization handlers then gate what that identified caller can do to threads, assistants, and crons.
optionExplanations.pa-q24-opt-b: Reverses the roles; permission decisions belong to authorization, while confirming credential validity is part of authentication.
optionExplanations.pa-q24-opt-c: Filtering which threads are visible is an authorization concern handled by resource-level handlers, not a description of authentication.
optionExplanations.pa-q24-opt-d: Authorization does not re-verify identity at all; it consumes the identity already established by authentication and applies permission logic to resources.

questions.takeaway: Authentication confirms who is making a request, while authorization decides what that already-identified caller may do.

questions.stem: Which of the following resources are scoped by returning a metadata filter dictionary (e.g. `{"owner": ctx.user.identity}`) from an `@auth.on` search or list handler? (Select all that apply.) (Select 3)

options.text: Threads
Assistants
Crons
Store
Deployment revisions
Docker build logs

optionExplanations.pa-q25-opt-a: Threads are scoped through the standard metadata-filter pattern, where a search or list handler returns a dictionary matched against thread metadata.
optionExplanations.pa-q25-opt-b: Assistants are also scoped through the standard metadata-filter pattern used by resource search and list handlers.
optionExplanations.pa-q25-opt-c: Crons follow the same metadata-filter pattern as threads and assistants for scoping search and list results.
optionExplanations.pa-q25-opt-d: The Store resource is authorized differently: its handlers rewrite the mutable `namespace` field to scope access, rather than returning a metadata filter dictionary.

optionExplanations.pa-q25-opt-f: Docker build logs are an infrastructure artifact from the build pipeline and are not a resource type that authorization handlers can scope access to.

questions.stem: During local development a team configures their agent with `durability="sync"` and `InMemorySaver` to test crash recovery. After killing and restarting the process, the thread's prior state is gone. Why?

options.text: `InMemorySaver` keeps checkpoints only in process memory, so restarting the process discards them regardless of the durability mode chosen.
`durability="sync"` was configured incorrectly, since sync mode requires `PostgresSaver` to function at all and silently falls back to no persistence.
The thread's `thread_id` was not passed on the restart call, which is the only reason `InMemorySaver` would appear to lose state.
Synchronous checkpoint writes are disabled by default for development builds, so no state was ever written in the first place.

questions.explanation: `InMemorySaver` keeps checkpoints only in process memory, so restarting the process discards them regardless of the durability mode chosen.

optionExplanations.pa-q26-opt-a: The durability mode only controls the timing of writes relative to graph execution; it does not change where the checkpointer stores data. An in-memory backend never survives a process restart no matter how synchronously it writes.
optionExplanations.pa-q26-opt-b: Sync mode works with any checkpointer implementation, including `InMemorySaver`; it does not require Postgres or silently disable itself when a different backend is used.
optionExplanations.pa-q26-opt-c: Even with the correct `thread_id` supplied, an in-memory backend has nothing to look up after a restart because the underlying process memory holding the checkpoints was cleared.
optionExplanations.pa-q26-opt-d: Durability modes are not disabled based on build type; the checkpoint writes did occur, they simply landed in memory that did not survive the process restart.

questions.takeaway: `InMemorySaver` keeps checkpoints only in process memory, so restarting the process discards them regardless of the durability mode chosen.

questions.stem: What does the checkpointer in LangGraph persist by default, and at what granularity does it write during a run?

options.text: A snapshot of graph state scoped to a thread, written at superstep boundaries as nodes complete their scheduled work.
Only the final output message of a run, written as one record once the entire graph execution finishes.
The full conversation across all of a user's threads, written any time any thread belonging to that user changes state.
The graph's static definition and configuration, written once at deployment time rather than during execution.

questions.explanation: A snapshot of graph state scoped to a thread, written at superstep boundaries as nodes complete their scheduled work.

optionExplanations.pa-q27-opt-a: A checkpointer captures thread-scoped graph state snapshots and writes them at superstep boundaries, which is the core mechanism enabling resumption and fault tolerance.
optionExplanations.pa-q27-opt-b: The checkpointer persists intermediate state throughout the run, not just a final output message, which is what allows recovery from mid-run failures.
optionExplanations.pa-q27-opt-c: This describes the store's cross-thread scope, not the checkpointer, which is deliberately scoped to a single thread.
optionExplanations.pa-q27-opt-d: The graph's code definition is not what the checkpointer persists; it persists runtime execution state, which changes throughout a run.

questions.takeaway: A snapshot of graph state scoped to a thread, written at superstep boundaries as nodes complete their scheduled work.
